analogy.p: Imagine a long tablecloth lying on a table with the table top slowly moving like a conveyor belt. The cloth (the plate) is carried along by the belt (the convection current in the mantle). At the edge of the table the cloth slides over the end and its weight pulls the rest of the cloth after it, which is **slab pull**. Where two cloths are pushed together, one slides under the other (subduction) or they crumple up (collision). The analogy breaks down because real plates are rigid slabs 100 km thick that are carried on very slowly flowing rock, and they can also be pushed away from a ridge by gravity (ridge push), which a tablecloth cannot show.
analogy.t: A tablecloth on a conveyor belt

bullets: **Inner core**: solid, made mainly of iron and nickel. It is the hottest layer (temperatures of around 5,000 °C or more) but it stays solid because of the enormous pressure.
**Outer core**: liquid iron and nickel, about 2,200 km thick. The movement of this liquid creates the Earth's magnetic field.

**Mantle**: the thickest layer, about 2,900 km. It is made of hot, dense rock that is **semi-molten**: it is mostly solid but it can flow very slowly over millions of years, a bit like very thick toothpaste. Temperatures range from a few hundred degrees at the top to around 3,000 °C at the base.
**Crust**: the thin, rigid outer layer. It is only about 5 to 10 km thick under the oceans and about 30 to 70 km thick under the continents.
The crust is cracked into huge slabs called **tectonic plates**. A plate is the crust plus the rigid very top of the mantle beneath it.
Heat in the core is partly left over from when the Earth formed and partly made by the decay of radioactive elements. This heat is the energy source that makes the mantle move.

Exam tip: if you are asked to label a diagram, learn the order from the outside in (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core) and one fact about each, such as 'liquid' for the outer core and 'solid' for the inner core.
core.p: The Earth is made of four main layers, and you must be able to describe each one. At the centre is the **inner core**, then the **outer core**, then the **mantle**, and on the outside the thin **crust** that we live on. The layers differ in thickness, temperature, state (solid or liquid) and what they are made of. Tectonic hazards happen because the heat deep inside the Earth drives movement in the mantle, and this moves the crust above it.

bullets: **Oceanic crust** is made mainly of basalt, a dark, heavy volcanic rock. Its density is about 3.0 g/cm³. It is constantly being made at constructive margins and destroyed at destructive margins, so it is never older than about 200 million years.

**Continental crust** is made mainly of granite-type rocks, which are lighter, with a density of about 2.7 g/cm³. It is too buoyant to be pulled down into the mantle, so it survives for billions of years.
Because oceanic crust is **denser**, it sinks (is **subducted**) beneath continental crust at destructive margins.
Where two continental plates meet, neither is dense enough to sink, so the crust crumples upwards instead.
Oceanic crust is **thinner** (5 to 10 km) than continental crust (30 to 70 km), which is why drilling or magma can reach the surface more easily on the ocean floor.
Link to rocks: the old continental crust is why the oldest rocks in the world are found on land, whereas the ocean floor is young everywhere.
core.p: There are two types of crust and the difference between them explains almost everything that happens at plate margins. **Oceanic crust** is thin, dense and relatively young. **Continental crust** is thicker, less dense and much older. When the two meet, density decides which one goes down, so this is a key idea for the exam. Remember that a plate can have both types, for example the South American plate has continental crust in the middle and oceanic crust at its eastern edge.

bullets: Evidence used by Wegener: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like a jigsaw; the same fossils (for example the freshwater reptile Mesosaurus) are found on continents now separated by ocean; matching rock types and mountain belts appear on opposite sides of the Atlantic.

Evidence from the ocean floor: the rock gets **older** the further it is from a mid-ocean ridge, and it forms symmetrical stripes of magnetic polarity either side of the ridge. This shows that new crust is being made at the ridge and the sea floor is **spreading**.
Plates are moving at roughly 2 to 10 cm per year, which has now been measured directly by satellites (GPS).
Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen at **plate margins** because that is where plates move against, away from or past each other.
A **plate margin** (or boundary) is the line where two plates meet. The type of margin depends on the direction of movement and the type of crust involved.
Do not describe the theory as 'the continents float on the sea'. The plates move over the semi-molten mantle, not on water.
core.h: Plate tectonics theory and the evidence for it
core.p: The theory of **plate tectonics** says that the Earth's crust is broken into a small number of large plates (7 major plates and many smaller ones) that move slowly over the mantle. They move at only a few centimetres a year, about the speed at which your fingernails grow, but over millions of years this moves continents thousands of kilometres. The idea grew from Alfred Wegener's **continental drift** hypothesis (1912), which suggested that all the continents were once joined in a supercontinent called **Pangaea** about 250 million years ago. At first scientists rejected it because Wegener could not explain how the continents moved. Evidence from the sea floor in the 1950s and 1960s finally showed that they do.

bullets: **Convection currents**: heat from the core makes mantle rock rise (less dense), move sideways beneath the plates, cool, then sink (more dense). The moving mantle drags the plates above it.

**Slab pull**: at a destructive margin the edge of the oceanic plate is old, cold and dense, so it sinks into the mantle under its own weight and pulls the rest of the plate behind it, like a tablecloth sliding off a table.

**Ridge push**: at a mid-ocean ridge the new crust is hot and sits higher than the older sea floor. Gravity makes the raised plate slide slowly downhill and away from the ridge, pushing the plate along.
Many geologists think slab pull is the strongest of the three, but mark schemes accept any of these three processes as causes of plate movement.
Convection currents alone do not fully explain plate movement. The mantle is not a liquid, so it is better to say rock 'flows very slowly' than 'is molten'.
Why it matters: plates are always moving, so stress builds up at the margins. When it is released suddenly you get an earthquake, and when magma reaches the surface you get a volcano.
core.h: Why do plates move? Convection currents, slab pull and ridge push
core.p: The spec names three processes that help to move plates, and you should be able to explain each of them. The heat from the core warms the mantle; the hot rock near the bottom becomes less dense and slowly rises, spreads out sideways under the crust, cools, becomes denser and sinks again. This circular flow is a **convection current**. The plates are carried along on top of these currents and are also pulled and pushed by their own weight, which is the idea behind slab pull and ridge push. Together these forces move the plates a few centimetres every year.

bullets: **Describe** the pattern using geography language: 'occur in linear bands', 'concentrated along plate margins', 'many surround the Pacific Ocean in the Ring of Fire', 'few in the centre of continents'. Use named places for extra marks.
**Volcanoes** are found at destructive margins (for example the Andes and Japan) and at constructive margins (for example Iceland and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge).
**Earthquakes** are found at all four types of margin, including conservative margins (San Andreas Fault, California) and collision margins (Himalayas), where there are no volcanoes.

Anomalies: a few volcanoes occur far from any plate margin, for example the Hawaiian islands in the middle of the Pacific plate. These are formed above a **hot spot**, a fixed plume of very hot magma rising through the mantle, while the plate moves over it.
A few earthquakes occur away from margins, for example from old faults inside a plate or triggered by human activity, but they are usually small.
Skills: if you are given a map, say where the pattern is, which plates are involved and give a few place names, then use a direction or distance for at least one place.
core.h: Global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes
core.p: On a world map, earthquakes and volcanoes are not spread randomly. They form narrow **belts** that follow the edges of the tectonic plates. The biggest belt is the **Pacific Ring of Fire**, a horseshoe of margins around the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes (about 90%) and a large share of the world's active volcanoes (about 75%) occur. Other belts run through the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, across the Mediterranean and Himalayas, and down the East African Rift. You need to be able to describe this pattern and link it to plate margins.

bullets: **Step 1**: two plates move towards each other (caused by convection currents and slab pull).
**Step 2**: the denser oceanic plate is forced down into the mantle under the continental plate. This is **subduction** and it creates a deep **ocean trench** at the surface.

**Step 3**: friction between the plates makes them stick. Pressure builds up for years, then is suddenly released as an **earthquake** when the plates jerk past each other. Subduction zone earthquakes can be very powerful (magnitude 8 to 9).
**Step 4**: as the oceanic plate sinks deeper the heat and pressure, and the water carried down in the plate, make it melt and form **magma**.

**Step 5**: magma is less dense than the surrounding rock, so it rises through cracks and vents and erupts at the surface as a **composite (strato) volcano**. The magma is thick and sticky (viscous) and full of gas, so eruptions are **explosive**.

**Landforms**: ocean trenches, composite volcanoes, volcanic island arcs (such as Japan and the Caribbean islands), and fold mountains on the continental side (such as the Andes) where sediment is crumpled.
**Hazards**: powerful earthquakes, explosive eruptions with ash clouds, pyroclastic flows and lahars, and tsunamis if the earthquake is under the sea.
core.h: Destructive margin: processes, landforms and hazards
core.p: At a **destructive (convergent) margin** two plates move **towards** each other and one is destroyed. This margin always involves at least one **oceanic plate**. The denser oceanic plate is forced beneath the lighter continental plate in a process called **subduction**. This is the most hazardous type of margin because it produces both very powerful earthquakes and explosive volcanoes. The classic AQA example is the Nazca plate (oceanic) subducting beneath the South American plate (continental), producing the Andes mountains and the Peru-Chile trench.

bullets: **Step 1**: convection currents (and ridge push) pull the plates apart.
**Step 2**: magma rises from the mantle into the gap because the pressure on it is reduced.
**Step 3**: the magma cools and solidifies to form new oceanic crust, which becomes part of the plates on each side. The oldest rock is furthest from the ridge.
**Landforms**: mid-ocean ridges, **shield volcanoes** (broad with gently sloping sides), and on land **rift valleys** such as the East African Rift.
The magma at constructive margins is **runny** (low viscosity) with little gas, so eruptions are **gentle** and frequent, with lava flowing a long way.
**Hazards**: frequent but small earthquakes (usually low magnitude and shallow) and lava flows. These are much less dangerous than at destructive margins.
Do not say that crust is 'destroyed' at constructive margins. It is **created** there, which is why the margin is called constructive.
core.h: Constructive margin: processes, landforms and hazards
core.p: At a **constructive (divergent) margin** two plates move **away** from each other and new crust is made. This happens mostly under the ocean along a **mid-ocean ridge**, the longest mountain chain on Earth. As the plates move apart, a gap opens, magma from the mantle rises to fill it, cools and solidifies as new crust. This process is called **sea-floor spreading**. The classic example is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates are moving apart and which comes above sea level in Iceland.

bullets: **Step 1**: two plates carrying continental crust are moved towards each other.
**Step 2**: because both are light and buoyant, neither sinks into the mantle. Sediment and rock between them is squeezed and folded.
**Step 3**: the crumpled crust is forced upwards to form **fold mountains**.

**Hazards**: earthquakes, which can be powerful because of the huge pressure that builds up as the plates are jammed together. There are **no volcanoes** (or very few), because no oceanic plate is subducted so no magma is formed.
Landforms: fold mountains (Himalayas, Alps). The Alps formed from the collision of the African and Eurasian plates.
This margin is sometimes grouped with destructive margins, but AQA treats it as a separate type, so name it 'collision'.
Common question: 'Why are there no volcanoes at collision margins?' because there is no subduction and so no melting to make magma.
core.h: Collision margin: processes, landforms and hazards
core.p: At a **collision margin** two **continental** plates move towards each other. Both have low density, so neither is subducted. Instead the edges of the plates are forced upwards and crumple, which builds high **fold mountains**. The best example is the Himalayas, where the Indian plate is colliding with the Eurasian plate. This collision began about 50 million years ago and is still going, which is why the Himalayas are still slowly rising and why the region has powerful earthquakes.

bullets: **Step 1**: the plates move past each other, so they are rubbing against each other along a crack called a fault.
**Step 2**: friction makes the plates stick. The plates still try to move, so pressure builds up.
**Step 3**: eventually the pressure overcomes the friction and the plates suddenly jerk past each other, sending out **seismic waves** that cause an earthquake.
Earthquakes at conservative margins are usually **shallow**, which means more shaking at the surface, so they can be very damaging near cities such as Los Angeles and San Francisco.
**Hazards**: earthquakes, plus secondary hazards such as landslides and fires from broken gas pipes. There are **no volcanoes** because no magma is formed and no crust is destroyed.
Landforms: few large landforms, but the fault itself can sometimes be seen as a long scar across the land, and rivers or roads can be offset sideways.
core.h: Conservative margin: processes, landforms and hazards
core.p: At a **conservative (transform) margin** the plates slide **past** each other, either in opposite directions or in the same direction at different speeds. No crust is made and none is destroyed, hence the name conservative. The plates do not move smoothly, because friction locks them together. Stress builds up for years until the rocks suddenly slip, releasing energy as a violent earthquake. The classic example is the **San Andreas Fault** in California, where the Pacific plate and the North American plate move in the same general direction but at different speeds.

bullets: **Focus** and **epicentre**: the focus is the origin of the earthquake underground, the epicentre is directly above it on the surface. A **shallow focus** (less than about 70 km) gives stronger shaking at the surface than a deep focus.
**Seismic waves** spread out from the focus in all directions. P (primary) waves are fastest, S (secondary) waves are slower, and surface waves arrive last but cause most of the damage.

**Magnitude** is measured with a **seismograph**. The **Richter scale** is a logarithmic scale: each whole number up means about **10 times** more ground shaking (amplitude) and about 32 times more energy. A magnitude 7 earthquake therefore has shaking 100 times greater than a magnitude 5.
Modern scientists mostly use the **moment magnitude scale** (similar numbers to Richter for large earthquakes). Questions normally say 'magnitude' only, so use the word magnitude.
The **Mercalli scale** measures the **effects** (intensity) of an earthquake on people and buildings (from I, barely felt, to XII, total destruction) instead of the energy released.
Earthquakes cannot be predicted accurately. Monitoring can show where they are likely (for example, along known faults) but not when.
core.h: Earthquakes: focus, epicentre, seismic waves and magnitude
core.p: An **earthquake** is a sudden release of energy in the Earth's crust that sends out vibrations called **seismic waves**. The point underground where the energy is released is the **focus**. The point on the surface directly above the focus is the **epicentre**. Shaking is strongest at the epicentre and gets weaker with distance. How damaging an earthquake is depends on its magnitude, its depth, the distance from people and the buildings.

bullets: **Composite (strato) volcano**: steep-sided cone built from alternating layers of ash and lava. Formed at destructive margins. Magma is thick and sticky (viscous), gas gets trapped, pressure builds and it erupts **explosively**. Examples: Mount St Helens, Mount Pinatubo.

**Shield volcano**: wide with gently sloping sides, built from many layers of runny lava. Formed at constructive margins and hot spots. Eruptions are **gentle** because gas escapes easily. Examples: Kilauea and Mauna Loa in Hawaii.
**Eruption products**: lava flows, ash and gas clouds, volcanic bombs, **pyroclastic flows** (fast, extremely hot clouds of ash, gas and rock) and **lahars** (mudflows of ash and water).
**Active** volcanoes have erupted recently and are likely to erupt again, **dormant** volcanoes are quiet but could erupt, and **extinct** volcanoes are not expected to erupt again.
Eruption warning signs include small earthquakes, ground swelling, and changes in gas emissions, which are covered in the monitoring and prediction topic.
Volcanic ash and gas can affect the climate. For example, the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo put so much material into the atmosphere that global temperatures fell by about 0.5 °C for a year or two.
core.h: Volcanoes: composite and shield volcanoes and eruptions
core.p: A **volcano** is a vent in the crust where **magma** (molten rock underground) reaches the surface and is erupted as **lava** (molten rock on the surface), ash and gases. There are two main types in the AQA course. The type of volcano and style of eruption are controlled by the **viscosity** of the magma (how thick and sticky it is) and how much gas it contains.

bullets: Always state the **direction of plate movement** (towards, away, past) and the **type of crust** involved (oceanic or continental). These two facts decide which margin it is.
Use a 'cause then effect' chain: because the oceanic plate is denser, it is subducted, which causes melting, which creates magma, which erupts as a volcano.

Summary table to learn: **Destructive** = towards, oceanic and continental, earthquakes and volcanoes. **Constructive** = apart, mostly oceanic, small earthquakes and gentle volcanoes. **Collision** = towards, both continental, earthquakes and fold mountains, no volcanoes. **Conservative** = past, any crust, earthquakes only.

Remember the examples with their plates: Nazca and South American (destructive), North American and Eurasian (constructive, Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Iceland), Indian and Eurasian (collision, Himalayas), Pacific and North American (conservative, San Andreas Fault).

Link to other topics: the **effects and responses** to a tectonic event (geo.0.2) are examined using case studies, **living in hazardous areas** (geo.0.3) explains why people stay, and **monitoring, prediction and planning** (geo.0.4) shows how hazards are managed.

Link to the risk equation: hazard risk is higher where a powerful hazard (such as a subduction zone) meets many vulnerable people, which is why Japan and Chile are at higher risk than parts of the Atlantic Ocean ridge.
core.h: Linking plate margins to hazards, and how to write about them
core.p: Questions on this topic usually ask you to describe the processes at a particular margin, explain why a landform or hazard occurs there, or use a diagram. The key to full marks is to give a clear **sequence**, use the correct terms (subduction, magma, friction, pressure) and include the **reason why** at each step. Practise drawing a labelled cross-section of each margin: a simple, neat sketch with arrows showing plate movement earns marks and helps you to remember the order.

exam: Command words: 'describe' means say what the pattern or process is (no reasons); 'explain' means give reasons using 'because' or 'so that'; 'suggest' means apply your knowledge to something you have not met.
A 1-mark question is usually a definition or a label (for example 'what is the focus of an earthquake?'). Give one precise fact.
A 2-mark 'describe the global distribution' answer: one mark for the pattern (bands along plate margins) and one for a named example (Ring of Fire).

A 4-mark 'explain how a composite volcano forms' answer needs a sequence of four linked points: plates move towards each other; oceanic plate subducted; melts and magma forms; magma rises and erupts building layers.
For 'explain' answers, write each point as a chain using 'which means' or 'so': 'The oceanic plate is denser, so it is subducted.'
Use named examples with plate names (Nazca plate and South American plate; Indian and Eurasian plates; Pacific and North American plates) to access higher marks.

A diagram question: draw a clear cross-section, label the plates, arrows for direction of movement, and key features (trench, magma, volcano, earthquake focus). Neat labelled sketches are worth marks in extended answers.
For a 6-mark compare answer (for example 'compare constructive and destructive margins'), write about similarities and differences in each paragraph, using words like 'whereas' and 'however'.
If given a map of plates or earthquakes, quote at least one place name or plate name from the map, and say 'concentrated', 'linear' or 'scattered' for the pattern.
Mention the type of magma and eruption style when asked about the volcano's hazard: viscous and explosive (destructive), runny and gentle (constructive).
Check you have answered the question that was asked: a 'describe processes' question does not need effects and responses.
Spell key terms correctly: subduction, convection, epicentre, magma, destructive, constructive, conservative. Misspelled terms can lose marks if the meaning is unclear.

mistakes.r: The plates move on the semi-molten mantle, which is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly; it is not a liquid.
mistakes.w: The plates float on liquid magma.

mistakes.r: Volcanoes form at destructive and constructive margins (and hot spots). Collision and conservative margins have earthquakes but no volcanoes.
mistakes.w: Volcanoes form at all plate margins.

mistakes.r: One plate (oceanic, denser) is subducted beneath the other; melting makes magma which forms volcanoes. Collision is a separate margin with two continental plates.
mistakes.w: At a destructive margin the plates collide and the land is pushed up.

mistakes.r: It sinks because it is denser. It melts because of the heat and pressure deeper in the mantle (and water in the plate), forming magma.
mistakes.w: The oceanic plate sinks because it is heavier, so it melts.

mistakes.r: New crust is made at a constructive margin as magma rises, cools and solidifies.
mistakes.w: Crust is destroyed at a constructive margin.

mistakes.r: Most do, but a few occur inside plates on old faults. Most, though, are on margins, so say 'most'.
mistakes.w: Earthquakes only happen at plate margins.

mistakes.r: Plates move a few centimetres per year, which is slow but adds up over millions of years.
mistakes.w: Plates move very quickly, so continents move every year.

mistakes.r: The Richter scale is logarithmic: each whole number is about 10 times more shaking.
mistakes.w: The Richter scale goes up in equal steps.

mistakes.r: Magma is molten rock underground; lava is molten rock that has reached the surface.
mistakes.w: Lava and magma are the same thing.

summary: You need to know the structure of the Earth, how and why tectonic plates move (convection currents, slab pull and ridge push), the global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes, and what happens at destructive, constructive, collision and conservative margins, including the landforms and hazards. It matters because it explains where tectonic hazards happen and underpins every case-study question on tectonic events.

terms.d: The thin, rigid outer layer of the Earth, about 5 to 10 km thick under oceans and 30 to 70 km under continents.
The thick layer of hot, semi-molten rock between the crust and the core; it flows very slowly.
A layer of liquid iron and nickel around the inner core.
The solid, very hot centre of the Earth, made mainly of iron and nickel.
A large slab of the Earth's crust (and uppermost mantle) that moves slowly over the mantle.
The boundary where two tectonic plates meet.
A slow circular flow in the mantle caused by heat: hot rock rises, spreads, cools and sinks.
The force of a cold, dense oceanic plate sinking at a subduction zone and pulling the rest of the plate with it.
The force that pushes a plate away from a mid-ocean ridge, because the new crust sits higher and slides downhill.
The process where a denser oceanic plate is forced down beneath another plate into the mantle.
A plate margin where plates move towards each other and oceanic crust is destroyed by subduction.
A plate margin where plates move apart and new crust is formed from rising magma.
A margin where two continental plates move together, crumpling the crust into fold mountains.
A margin where plates slide past each other; crust is neither made nor destroyed.
Mountains formed when the crust is squeezed and crumpled where plates collide.
A deep, narrow valley in the sea floor where an oceanic plate is subducted.
A steep-sided volcano made of layers of ash and lava, formed at destructive margins, with explosive eruptions.
A wide, gently sloping volcano formed from runny lava, found at constructive margins and hot spots.
Molten rock beneath the Earth's surface.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake.

worked.ans: Model answer: At a destructive margin the denser oceanic plate moves towards the continental plate and is forced beneath it in a process called subduction (1). As the plate sinks it melts due to the heat and pressure in the mantle, forming magma (1). The magma is less dense than the rocks around it so it rises through cracks and vents (1). It erupts onto the surface and, after many eruptions, layers of ash and lava build up to form a steep-sided composite volcano (1).
worked.q: Explain how a composite volcano is formed at a destructive plate margin. [4 marks]
steps: Identify the margin: an oceanic plate and a continental plate are moving towards each other.
Say what happens: the denser oceanic plate is forced down under the continental plate (subduction).
Explain melting: as it sinks it melts because of the heat and pressure, forming magma.
Explain eruption: the magma is less dense so it rises through cracks and vents to the surface and erupts. Repeated eruptions build up layers of ash and lava to form a steep cone.

worked.ans: Model answer: Earthquakes and volcanoes mostly occur in narrow belts rather than being spread evenly across the world (1). These belts follow the boundaries of tectonic plates (1). A large number surround the Pacific Ocean in the 'Ring of Fire', for example along the west coast of South America and in Japan (1).
worked.q: Describe the global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes. [3 marks]
steps: Give the overall pattern: they occur in narrow belts or lines, not randomly.
Link to plate margins: these follow the edges of tectonic plates.
Add a named example: the Ring of Fire around the Pacific Ocean, or the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

worked.ans: Model answer: The plates slide past each other in different directions or at different speeds (1). Friction locks them together, so pressure builds up over time (1). When the pressure is suddenly released the plates jerk past each other, sending out seismic waves that cause an earthquake (1). There are no volcanoes because no crust is destroyed or created, so no magma is formed (1). Example: the San Andreas Fault.
worked.q: Describe what happens at a conservative plate margin, and state why there are no volcanoes there. [4 marks]
steps: Direction of movement: plates slide past each other, either in different directions or in the same direction at different speeds.
Friction: the plates lock together and pressure builds up.
Release: when the pressure overcomes friction, the plates jerk past each other causing an earthquake.
No volcanoes: crust is neither created nor destroyed so no magma is formed.
